story_text.value:
Hi HN! We're releasing an open-source CLI for hillclimbing Agent Experience. That means optimizing your agent-facing surfaces (Skills, CLIs, SDKs, and docs) so that your users' coding agents can easily use your product. Pointing your own agent at the repo is enough to get started. https://github.com/gauge-sh/gauge-cli

We've found that power users generally want to hand a CLI/MCP to their agents and get started from the terminal. They rarely want to log in and use the web UI themselves. We think developer tools must be agent-friendly to remain relevant.

Here are some common findings that Gauge identifies:

- agents get confused with CLI/SDK behavior and start source diving - interactive commands block agents - agents use deprecated/old CLI commands - agents don't use Skills when you'd expect - agents confidently assert limitations that don't exist - inconsistent terminology confuses agents - agents can't figure out how commands fit together into a workflow

Locally, the Gauge CLI uses Docker containers to run agent harnesses (you can bring your own subscriptions). It finds where agents get confused or stuck and tests changes using your pre-release artifacts (Skills/CLI etc). We normalize events from Claude Code, Codex, Pi and OpenCode into standardized transcripts, and store them locally, alongside structured information in SQLite so that your agent can easily analyze the data. This enables automatic hillclimbing toward a great Agent Experience.

We also offer hosted compute that enables more features, built on our custom Gateway (for credential brokering and transparent, per-session response rewriting). Hosted compute enables many more concurrent sessions, easier collaboration with teammates, a GitHub App for PR reviews, sessions with logged-in MCPs/APIs, and most importantly it lets you close your laptop while the sessions actually run.

You don't need a Gauge account to run the full loop end-to-end though. We expect that local execution with the CLI is enough to find and fix several agent experience issues in a typical project.

You'll be able to validate fixes for these issues locally, before publishing new versions (we inject pre-release Skills and code artifacts into the sessions).

We would love your feedback!

story_text.value:
What’s up HN?! I'm Benji, and I’ve been building Frink since ~April this year.

Frink is a desktop-first, open-source (MIT) app for running coding agents in parallel and multi-step workflows that start on their own. It runs on your machine (macOS and Linux) with your own provider login. It currently supports Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Copilot, and OpenCode, but the latter 3 are in preview. No Frink account to use the app.

The biggest USP of Frink is workflows: think n8n for agents. You describe a routine in a sentence, for example: "every weekday at 9am, run the tests; if any fail, have an agent fix them, then wait for my approval before it opens a PR." Then, Frink builds it as a workflow (or simply, Flow): a list of steps you can read and change before it runs. A Flow can start on a schedule, from any webhook, or from an event from a third-party such as Linear, Shortcut, ClickUp, Sentry, PostHog, etc. Steps can be agent turns, shell commands, conditions, approval steps that stop and wait for you, or steps you write yourself in code (or ask the agent to write one). Everything that needs you (an approval, an agent's question, a finished task to review) lands in one Work Queue.

Other stuff:

* Up to four agents side by side, each on its own git worktree if you want. Or, many agents out of direct view.

* Every change shows as a diff; there's a code editor, a terminal, etc.

* Local-first: chats, Flows and tasks live in SQLite on your machine.

* Easier provider parity: currently working on and improving the tooling setup between providers. Once inside Frink, irrespective of what provider you use, the hooks, MCPs, and other tooling work out of the box between providers.

Why I built it: I started building it when there weren’t many other competitors; now the industry is swamped with ADEs and harnesses. However, in my opinion, each still lacks good automation for more fine-tuned scenarios. I doubled down on the flows to help me with my actual day-to-day job as a SWE, and over time it’s helped me automate most of the PRs being shipped across my personal projects, team, etc., to the point that it’s a continuous loop and helps a whole ton.

Notes: Windows isn't supported yet. Flows only run on Claude Code and Codex for now. It's a solo project, so expect sharp edges.

story_text.value:
I often switch between Claude Code and Codex throughout the week, and between my laptop and an older machine I leave running at home. I built agent-archive to make it easier to pick up where I left off, especially when i hit usage limits.

It lets you (or a coding agent) find past coding sessions and hand their conversation context to another agent. You can try local handoffs without setup, or connect your own S3/R2 bucket for automatic archiving and access from other machines.

It also tracks usage across agents and gives you a full archive of your session transcripts across agents, which I've found useful to iterating and improving my AGENTS.md and lint rules.

story_text.value:
I run long sessions with Claude. For a long time I've had Claude in the middle of some difficult coding task, and then I see the auto-compact message pop up. Every time I wonder if Claude actually picks everything up correctly and nothing is lost. Claude told me 78/82 auto-compactions landed while Claude was working. For a while I couldn't do much. At first I made a skill that would make Claude explicitly save progress throughout long runs. But that didn't fix the core problem and cost more tokens as well. Now that mods came out, I fixed the actual problem.

catnap tells Claude at 50% context what the context is and that it should finish what it's working on, write a handoff, and then initialize compaction itself. When Claude finishes its task, catnap compacts, and Claude can then pick up work again. The handoff replaces Claude Code's default summary, so we don't do similar work twice. If Claude for some reason doesn't compact before 60%, it gets a stricter note. And Claude Code's default auto-compact kicks in at 70% as a backstop. The 3 numbers are all settings.

After I took on catnap, 0 of 129 naps came mid-task: 98 of them in benchmarks and 31 in my own sessions.

The cost is the same as the default auto-compact kicking in at the same point, in tokens and dollars, on 200K and 1M context windows. Compared to the default auto-compaction that kicks in when context is nearly full, catnap used 56% fewer tokens. But lowering the default auto-compact will get you most of the way there as well.

I measured memory today as well. Claude worked through tasks one message at a time while 20 instructions and facts were said in the chat, inside long chatty messages, and nowhere else. Asked right after compaction to list them from memory, no file reads: all 20 were listed with catnap and with the default compaction, in every run (15 with catnap, 5 with the default). So in my tests the memory was exactly the same, but catnap got there with a handoff 60% shorter (4.0K tokens against 10K).

I was surprised that catnap is actually faster than the default option. This wasn't even one of the reasons I wanted to make this, it just happened. Since Claude writes the handoff in one go instead of the separate summary call the default makes, and the note is shorter, tasks finish sooner: measured end to end, 406 seconds instead of 464.

Try it with nothing installed:

  npx github:LippInc/catnap
It prints how often auto-compact cut in mid-task in your own logs (reads numbers only, sends nothing).

Install (needs Claude Code 2.1.287 or later, where mods are on by default):

  claude plugin marketplace add LippInc/catnap
  claude plugin install catnap@lippinc
Currently Claude Code only, tested on Windows and Linux. The memory test used made-up coding tasks on a 200K window.

Some related tools: compact-adviser, handoff-compact, session-pilot and sub-agent-compact. What catnap adds: Claude finishes its piece first, and the numbers on where the cut lands.

title.value: Show HN: Stop Claude Code from compacting mid-task

story_text.value:
I built a quiz game around TypeSafe's new Jev model, which has vision capabilities. Jev looks at a picture and a question and picks an answer (or taps a place) in about a quarter of a second.

I've always loved quiz games and thought this would be a fun way to see what it can do and how fast it is. I made the cards from scratch, and Jev gets exactly the picture you see. More cards will come over time.

Play against Jev on your own (there's a leaderboard for each mode), or start a live match and challenge your friends, with Jev as one more player.

The code is open source, so feel free to build your own game or make more cards that I can publish.

Play: https://jevcards.com Code: https://github.com/Jose-Sabater/jevcards (the newest cards stay private for a while)

Disclaimer: I ran Jev through both TypeSafe and Opper, and made the cards through Opper's vision models and Claude Code. I work at Opper, but jevcards is open source and free to play.

story_text.value:
I've been considering subscribing to a bundle from one of the purveyors of AI coding tools.

I currently have access to ChatGPT Pro, GitHub Copilot, etc. I've used Claude Code, but can't really distinguish the vibes between the models. However, I often run out of tokens at the "Plus" plan levels even when using GPT-6.1-Sol as my daily driver.

I'm considering Google Antigravity Ultra at the $100 tier. It also seems to include a generous rate limits and quota for their models and series of extra features including: cloud storage, YouTube Premium, etc.

I figure that if the Google models don't perform as well as the "frontier" labs then I can always supplement with $20 plans and have the Anti-gravity tooling use the more capable models as orchestrators and use subagents.

What do folks think, what's the best value for the money bundle out there right now?

story_text.value:
Hi HN,

I'm John, a knowledge management and AI enablement professional. I created Standard Topic, an AI and RSS-powered news and resource platform, with assistance from Claude Code.

Standard Topic uses AI integrations and RSS feeds to curate news and resources across relevant topics and presents these in the form of top stories, trending items, and a curated prompt library to easily gather further context on a given topic (examples of topics being World News, Politics, Business, Technology, Sports, Science, Health and more.)

On topic hubs, you can find a regularly updated at-a-glance AI briefings providing relevant updates, top stories with AI insights and cited sources, and additional recent news coverage. A governance system is in place with AI assisting in ranking stories, retiring items from the top stories section, determining which additional news is displayed, and more.

An AI-generated briefing podcast, in the format of a radio news program, releases each morning and evening (5 AM and 5 PM ET), covering the latest global news.

While in the past I've released apps and websites that felt duct-taped together and which I stopped using after some time, with this one I've actually found myself using it more than Twitter/X and other daily news briefing platforms, while also leading me to more frequently engage directly with publishing platforms cited on Standard Topic.

My recent work in AI has been around finding practical uses in the content and knowledge management areas for integrating the technology, and Standard Topic has developed into what I see as a product that uses structured outputs and automated insights to deliver consistent and trustworthy, cited content while maintaining transparency about being primarily powered by artificial intelligence.

There's still some kinks to work out in terms of automated workflows, design aspects and more.

Let me know what you think!
